unison

/YOO-nuh-sun/ — stress on first syllable · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Unison is the act of doing or saying something together, at exactly the same time as others.

The rowers pulled in perfect unison, eight oars striking the water as one.

Example

When the orchestra's strings entered the symphony, all fifty violins moved their bows in unison, creating a single, shimmering sound.

Unison emphasizes the simultaneity and perfect synchronization—every violin moving at exactly the same moment, in the same way. You could say 'together,' but unison is more precise because it means not just at the same time, but doing the identical action.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

accord: Accord is a state of agreement between people — two sides that share an opinion or settle a dispute are in accord. It lives in minds, not in movement. Unison lives in action: voices or bodies doing the identical thing at the identical instant, whatever anyone privately thinks.

chorus: A chorus is many voices delivering the same words together — the word points at who is acting: a whole group speaking or singing as one. Unison points at how the action matches: identical and exactly simultaneous. A crowd can answer in chorus yet still be slightly out of unison.

lockstep: Lockstep is exact, matched movement, like soldiers marching, and it often carries a criticism — people copying one another without thinking for themselves. Unison is the neutral word for doing the identical thing at the identical moment, and it usually admires the precision instead of mocking it.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

discord: clashing disagreement among sounds or people

chaos: a jumbled state with no order or shared timing

Where it sits · how exactly the actions match in time

together → harmony → synchrony → unison

together vs. unison: Together is the weakest of these: it only means people are doing something with each other, while unison demands that every action happen at exactly the same instant.

harmony vs. unison: Harmony is stronger than simply being together, but still gentler than unison — in harmony, different parts blend pleasingly, while unison requires everyone to do the very same thing at the very same time.

synchrony vs. unison: Synchrony comes closest to unison: both involve matched timing, but unison is the strongest term because the actions are not just timed together — they are identical, as if performed by one body.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — uni-: one (Latin)

Root — son: sound (Latin)

Put it together: Uni- ('one') plus son ('sound') literally means 'one sound' — and that is exactly what unison is: many voices or actions matching so precisely that they sound and move as one.

Use the root in a new word: sonic: The jet's sonic boom rattled every window on the block.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral

Unison is the precise word when you mean not just simultaneous action, but identical action happening at the exact same moment. Reach for it when describing groups moving together as one unit. For looser coordination or timing, the simpler word 'together' works fine.
